title: Zenkei Blanche Hartman
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Blanche Hartman shares her personal experience of meeting Suzuki Roshi, who taught her that true understanding comes from embracing one's imperfections and limitations. Through private interviews with Roshi, she learned to cultivate self-awareness and humility, recognizing that spiritual growth requires a willingness to let go of ego and misconceptions about oneself. This lesson has stayed with Hartman, offering valuable insights into the importance of acknowledging others' worth and value with respect and gratitude, particularly as we age.

sentences.text: *This is from an interview that Blanche Hartman had with David Chadwick in 1995.
She said, "When I first came to Zen Center* (which is San Francisco Zen Center, it's the custom there to just call it Zen Center) *when I first came to Zen Center my life was shaky.
Our marriage was shaky and we had been to a marriage counselor and I learned things about the dynamics between myself and my family that made me feel really bad about myself.
It was 1968.

I met Suzuki Roshi in '69 and in the first lecture I heard him give, he said, 'You're perfect just as you are.' And I thought, 'Well, he doesn't know me very well.' But I kept going to his lectures and he kept saying things like that.
'You have everything you need.
There's nothing lacking.
You're complete as you are.' It finally got through to me that he actually was including me because he wasn't leaving anybody out.
He was including all of us.
Then I had to deal with that.
What was this really meaning?
What was he really talking about?
This became a real question for me, a koan, and I've come to see that that is the primary teaching of the Buddha.*
*When I started sitting, it was like a drowning person grabbing a life preserver.
I was sitting every morning and afternoon at the Berkeley Zendo and my daughters complained that I was never home, but I had no choice.
Suzuki Roshi came to the Berkeley Zendo every Monday morning and a bunch of us went with him, a bunch of us went to the city for his Wednesday night and Saturday talks and sittings.
I was going to one-day sittings but I didn't go to Dokusan, interview with him, for at least six months because I felt so bad about myself.
I didn't want to expose myself to him.
Finally, my friend Meg Goller said, 'Go see him anyway,' so I did.
One of the things that impressed me about it: I was so devoted to him and very happy that I got to bow to him.

Then when I sat down, I had made this black skirt for sittings, I was arranging the skirt and he said, 'Oh, you're arranging your skirt so carefully because of how much you respect me and respect the Dharma.' He could see that I bowed with a great deal of feeling and he said, 'Well, you know, if you just touch your head three times when you bow, it's like you're bowing to me three times instead of one.' It was an unusual thing to say.
He could have said that our custom is to touch our head three times to the floor when we bow but instead he picked up on my attitude towards him and used it as a way to teach me.*
*I went to Tassajara a few days after I'd first had Zazen instruction, and Tassajara is our monastery, so kind of an intense place to go.
I fell in love with the place and I went right back down as soon as I got time off for a training period.
My roommate was Meg Goller and I wasn't sure it was okay for a woman over 45 to be there.
All the other students were like 20."* I was trying to see this the other night.
Yeah, she was 45.

*"Only Katherine Tanis, Pat Herashoff and I were that age and there was a sprinkling of people in their 30s but everyone else was in their 20s, most of them early 20s and it didn't seem like they wanted anyone around.
I looked like their mothers.
But Meg made me feel welcome and I was totally grateful to her.
When I left, she said, 'Don't forget to send care packages.' At that time, there wasn't any back door to the kitchen like now where they have snacks.
There were no snacks and the kitchen was macrobiotic and they didn't feed you very much food.
So I sent lots of cookies.
Every time someone would go to Tassajara, I'd send more cookies.
And then at a certain point, I thought, 'How come she doesn't send a letter to me and tell me how great I am for sending all those cookies?' And then I thought, 'How selfish I am.
This is not true generosity.
There are strings attached to my cookies.

I want something back.' So I went to see Suzuki Roshi and told him about it and he said, 'It's all right for you to take care of her but first you have to take care of yourself.' He said this in a rising voice and then he got right in my face and said very loudly, 'Do you understand?'"*
And a side note for me on that: Japanese teachers that I met would often say that.
They'd sprinkle their talks with "Do you understand?"
It seemed like this really profound question, like, do you really understand?
But then one time I was trying to give a dharma talk in Spanish and I really had no idea if I was making any sense.
So I asked them in Spanish, "Do you understand?"
And they realized, well, that's actually part of what's going on here.
They actually didn't know.
Does this person understand what I'm trying to say in this funny language?
Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah.
"Comprendas?"
So anyway, who knows what he meant.
I thought of that one time when I was giving that talk, like, oh.
*"And I jumped back and said, 'Yes!' And when I got out of there I thought, 'No, no, take care of yourself?
To take care of yourself is selfish.
Zen is about no self.' But I'd said yes and he's* [unclear: "his en master"]*, so I have to mean it.
And that became another koan for me and it still is.
What self do you take care of and how do you take care of others?*
*At the end of that Dokusan I got up to leave.
I wasn't very clear about the form, but I thought you just got up and you fluffed your cushion, you stepped back and bowed.
But there was a whole zafu and zabuton between me and Suzuki Roshi and I wanted to bow to him directly.
So I stepped forward and bowed with my head right down by the corner of his zabuton.
And when I stood up suddenly somehow he was head to head with me.
While I was bowing he had jumped up from his seat and bowed to me too.
I walked out of there stunned.
I knew that however much I respected him, he was meeting that respect with just as much respect for me and I couldn't believe it.*
*And another Dokusan,* [unclear: "Liu"] *and our daughter Trudy had begun sitting and I was always going up there telling him what an awful person I was and how awful I felt about myself.
What a bad member of my family I was.
But Suzuki Roshi was always so encouraging.
And that day he said, 'You know, sometimes I look out of the window and I see you and your daughter walking down the street arm-in-arm and it's so wonderful.
You and your husband and your daughter are sitting together.
It doesn't always happen like that.
Sometimes when a wife begins to sit the husband gets jealous, like she has a new boyfriend.
But it's because of your deep sincerity that they can practice with you.
It's because of your love for the practice.' It's so encouraging to me when I was down on myself.*
*But on the other hand, one time I'd been sitting one day counting my breath and I finally got into it.
Finally.
Period after period it seemed like I could count every breath and my mind never strayed.
I went to see him in Dokusan, so happy and so proud of myself.
I said, 'Well, now I can count every breath.
Now I can do it.
What do I do next?' He leaned forward and he said to me very fiercely and sternly,* I remember her telling the story to me, *'Don't ever think you sit zazen.
That's a big mistake.
Zazen sits zazen.
Only zazen.'* I was so impressed by that.
When she told me, she was kind of horrified by it too.
*"That was the first time I'd gone to him feeling proud of myself and he helped me a lot."*
It reminds me of Jack Kornfield's story of going to his teacher and complaining that he was inconsistent, telling different people different things.

And the teacher said, "Oh well, it's because when I see somebody on the road about to fall in the ditch on the right I say go left, and then I see somebody else about to fall in a ditch on the left so I say go right."
*"In that way, when I felt discouraged Suzuki Roshi was very encouraging.
He was very encouraging when I was discouraged and when I was feeling proud he would knock me down.
There's one thing that happened that's very embarrassing but it's indicative of how he taught me.

Right after we moved into the building,"* this is the San Francisco Zen Center, this big beautiful building designed by a famous architect, I don't know how they got it, but anyway, *"right after we moved into the building I was still smoking.
It was during a sesshin, a formal retreat.
But things were a bit looser then.
People would go down to Kirby's for ice cream during the breaks and goof off.
And nowadays when you prepare an offering tray for the food we offer in the Buddha Hall, before the meals they do this offering.
It's received from the kitchen with great respect and solemnity and it represents an offering from those working in the kitchen to those practicing in the Zendo.
But in those days we were a bit casual and we didn't understand the form very well.
But what I did was nevertheless really off the wall.
It was sort of like going to the opera in only my Maidenform bra.
What I did was I went out to get the offering tray and it was just before noon service and Suzuki Roshi had been upstairs during Dokusan and he hadn't come down yet.
So I figured I had time to have a cigarette.

So I lit the cigarette and I was carrying the offering tray in one hand and the cigarette in the other and he saw me and he looked at me and he paused and he waggled his finger and he continued in to the Zendo.
That waggling finger came back to me when I was quitting smoking five years later and having a terrible time of it, and that wagging finger was the greatest help I ever had in quitting smoking."*
So there's some memories from our ancestor Zenkei Blanche Hartman, who was a big help to me when I was first practicing as a young man at San Francisco Zen Center.
And it's so interesting, you know, we were always talking to somebody about aging the other day.
Have you been thinking about aging too lately?
Isn't it strange that this could somehow be 30 years later and she's dead and I'm wearing the same outfit that she was wearing back then, talking about her, when I saw her talking about Suzuki Roshi.
I felt a little bit concerned though when I was offering here that absolution of karma.
I thought, who am I to offer Blanche absolution of karma, just some kid?
I felt 20 again in that moment.
I told this story the other day but it bears repeating.

One of the customs at Green Gulch, which we also do at our residential sesshin at Samish Island, which is coming up (we should go), is that when you pass somebody in the path, you stop and you silently acknowledge each other by stopping, standing still and bowing to each other.
You kind of bow like this to each other.

But of course, like all human beings, people got busy and there were things to do and things to pick up and jobs are happening and people are zipping around the place, like you would be, think about your house.
And so a lot of people got a little kind of pro forma with [unclear: "this little battle"] and kept running, doing all the stuff.
And Blanche would always really stop and bow very deeply and really pause.
I thought, why is she doing that to me?
I'm not very important.
But of course it isn't about that.
It's not about being important, it's about bowing, it's about meeting.
The other thing I was just thinking is where in our school you can tell who's been to do the training period at Tassajara: when we do the Daihishin Dharani, that chant that we did in this service.
At Tassajara in the 90-day training period you chant that every single day, at least once, sometimes twice, and it's a long thing full of nonsense syllables, right?
Doesn't make any sense, and you can't exactly memorize nonsense, really.
But that's not nonsense, but you know what I mean.
Somehow after going to Tassajara it's in there, and so if I don't think about it, if I just open my mouth and let those sounds come out, it's all in there.
I can't say exactly that I memorized it, but somehow the practice put it in there and it comes out when it's needed.
The time that I was at Tassajara I only did one training period there.
Some people do dozens.
My friend Charlie lived there for 17 years.
But anyway, Blanche was the teacher there when I did that training period, and so I was with her when I learned that.
So it felt good to chant that.
I stumbled a few times over the words and that felt good too, because she would stumble.
She was uncomfortable being the teacher of the training period and she really saw herself as kind of a background person, never too sure of herself, which is good for us.
She would give these talks where she would spend half the talk talking about how hard it had been for her to prepare for the talk.
She'd say, "I was in my room [unclear: "out of these books"] and like, what am I supposed to say?
How do you give these talks?
I'm not wise."
But it was just the right talk.
It was just so humble and sweet and just sharing herself and her process.
Of course part of me wanted wise, brilliant talks, but part of me knew this is just the right teacher for me, the right kind of talk for me to hear.
It's not about being somebody special.
She really took to heart what [unclear: "Susie Kirishu"] told her in 1968: it's okay to just be who we are, do what we can do, and maybe we'll stumble.
Definitely we'll stumble, and if we don't stumble we're probably not really being ourself anyway.
So I'm honored to get to give a memorial talk for one of my old teachers, [unclear: "saying Kate Mullen-Chartman"].
Let's spend the last couple of minutes of the talk just sitting, and just maybe we can complete whatever in this reflection speaks to you, and just feel whatever that is.
What's the feeling of that?
